Termite Inspection Cost: What to Expect in Kansas (2024)

By Shaw's Pest Control  ·  Wichita, KS

How Much Does a Termite Inspection Cost?

If you're trying to figure out what a termite inspection actually costs, you're probably either buying or selling a home, spotted something that looks like termite damage, or you're just being smart about protecting your property. The short answer: termite inspection cost in Kansas typically ranges from free to around $150, depending on what type of inspection you need and who's doing it. But there's more to the story than just the price tag. Some companies offer free inspections with strings attached, while others charge upfront for a thorough Wood-Destroying Insect (WDI) report required for real estate transactions. At Shaw's Pest Control, we've been inspecting homes across Wichita and the surrounding Kansas communities since 1987, and we've seen how confusing this process can be for homeowners. This guide breaks down exactly what you're paying for, what a professional inspection should include, and when you might need to budget for follow-up treatment.

What a Professional Termite Inspection Actually Covers

A legitimate termite inspection isn't someone walking through your house for five minutes and calling it good. A thorough inspection should take 45 minutes to an hour for an average-sized home, and it includes both interior and exterior assessments. The inspector should be checking your basement or crawlspace, examining foundation walls, inspecting wooden structures in contact with soil, looking at window frames and door jambs, and checking attic spaces where accessible.

They're looking for three main things: active termite activity (live insects, mud tubes, fresh frass), existing termite damage (hollowed wood, sagging floors, blistered wood surfaces), and conditions that make your home vulnerable to future infestation (moisture problems, wood-to-soil contact, excessive mulch against the foundation). A proper inspection should also identify the species if termites are present—subterranean termites are the primary concern in Kansas, and they require different treatment approaches than drywood termites common in other regions.

The inspector should provide you with a detailed report documenting their findings, including photos when possible. At Shaw's Pest Control, our technicians hold three State Certifications and Master Tech Certification, which means they've been trained to spot signs the average homeowner—or even less experienced inspectors—might miss.

Free Inspections vs. Paid Inspections: What's the Difference?

Many pest control companies advertise free termite inspections, and some of those are legitimate. But it's important to understand what you're getting and what the company's motivation is. Free inspections are often marketing tools—the company is hoping to find a problem and sell you treatment. That doesn't automatically make them dishonest, but it does mean you should pay attention to how they present their findings.

A free inspection typically covers the basics: a visual assessment of accessible areas and a report on whether termites are present. If you're just concerned about whether you have an active problem, a free inspection can be perfectly adequate—especially if you're working with an established, locally owned company with a reputation to protect.

Paid inspections, on the other hand, are usually more detailed and come with formal documentation. The main reason you'd pay for an inspection is when you need a WDI (Wood-Destroying Insect) report for a real estate transaction. Lenders and title companies often require these official reports before closing. A WDI report costs typically between $75 and $150 in Kansas, and it's a formal document that certifies the condition of the property. This report is legally binding and must follow specific state guidelines for what's inspected and how findings are reported.

If you're buying a home, your lender will usually specify whether they require a WDI report. If you're selling, your buyer's lender might require one before they'll approve the loan. These inspections must be conducted by licensed professionals, and the report is only valid for a limited time—usually 30 to 90 days—so timing matters when you're in a real estate transaction.

What Triggers a Treatment Recommendation (and What It Costs)

Finding evidence of termites doesn't automatically mean you need a $2,000 treatment tomorrow. A good inspector will explain exactly what they found and what level of response it requires. If there's active termite activity—live insects, fresh mud tubes, or recent damage—you'll need treatment fairly quickly to prevent further destruction.

If the inspector finds old damage with no signs of current activity, you might not need immediate treatment, but you should consider preventive measures and schedule regular monitoring. Some inspectors will recommend treatment for conditions conducive to termites (like moisture problems or wood-to-soil contact) even without active infestation—that's where you need to use your judgment and possibly get a second opinion.

Treatment costs vary widely based on the size of your home, the extent of infestation, and the treatment method. Liquid barrier treatments typically run $1,200 to $3,000 for an average home, while bait station systems might cost $1,500 to $3,500 for installation plus annual monitoring fees. Your termite control options depend on your specific situation, and a reputable company will explain why they're recommending a particular approach rather than just pushing the most expensive option.

The key question to ask: "Would you recommend this treatment if this were your own home?" If the inspector hesitates or gives you a sales pitch instead of a straight answer, that's a red flag.

Termite Inspections in the Wichita Area

Wichita homeowners face particular challenges when it comes to termites. Kansas soil conditions and our climate—with wet springs and hot summers—create ideal environments for subterranean termites. Older homes in established Wichita neighborhoods often have foundation designs that make them more vulnerable, including crawlspaces with inadequate ventilation and wooden support structures in direct soil contact.

If you're buying a home built before 1990 in the Wichita metro area, a termite inspection isn't optional—it's essential due diligence. Even newer construction can have problems if builders didn't follow proper prevention practices during construction. Local pest control companies familiar with termite control in Wichita understand regional termite behavior and know which neighborhoods and home styles face higher risk. That local knowledge matters when you're trying to determine whether a finding is a minor issue or a serious problem.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much does a termite inspection cost in Kansas?

Termite inspection costs in Kansas range from free to approximately $150. Basic inspections for homeowner peace of mind are often free from reputable pest control companies. Official WDI (Wood-Destroying Insect) reports required for real estate transactions typically cost $75–$150. The inspection should include interior and exterior assessment, crawlspace or basement inspection, and a detailed written report of findings and recommendations.

What does a WDI report include?

A WDI report is an official document that identifies any evidence of wood-destroying insects, including termites, carpenter ants, and powder post beetles. The report documents current infestations, past damage, and conditions conducive to future infestation. It must be performed by a licensed pest control professional and follows state-specific guidelines. These reports are valid for 30–90 days and are commonly required by mortgage lenders during home purchases or refinancing.

How long does a termite inspection take?

A thorough termite inspection takes 45 minutes to an hour for an average-sized home. The inspector examines the foundation, crawlspace or basement, interior rooms, attic spaces, and exterior perimeter. Larger homes or properties with multiple structures take longer. Be wary of inspections that take less than 30 minutes—they're likely missing important areas or rushing through the assessment without proper attention to detail.

Are free termite inspections worth it?

Free termite inspections can be worthwhile if conducted by licensed, reputable professionals. Many established pest control companies offer free inspections as a customer service, knowing that only a percentage of homes will have problems requiring treatment. The key is choosing a company with strong local reputation and proper certifications rather than national chains known for high-pressure sales tactics. Always ask what the inspection includes and whether you'll receive a written report of findings.

When should I get a termite inspection?

Get a termite inspection when buying or selling a home, if you notice signs of termite activity (mud tubes, hollow-sounding wood, discarded wings), every 2–3 years as preventive maintenance, before finishing a basement or major renovation, or if neighbors have had termite problems. Spring is peak swarming season in Kansas when termites are most visible, but inspections can be conducted year-round since subterranean termites remain active even in winter.

What happens if termites are found during an inspection?

If termites are found during an inspection, the inspector will document the location, extent of activity, and species identified. You'll receive treatment recommendations based on the severity of infestation. For real estate transactions, the purchase agreement typically specifies who pays for treatment—buyer, seller, or negotiated split. Active infestations require treatment before most lenders will approve a mortgage. Your inspector should provide a detailed treatment proposal with cost estimates before any work begins.
